subject: Civil Engineering
title: Critical Flow and Hydraulic Jumps
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Critical Flow and Hydraulic Jumps.

hook.text: Water at the base of a dam spillway flows insanely fast. Then it suddenly leaps upward.

buildup.text: Supercritical flow is fast and shallow. Subcritical flow is slow and deep.

discovery.text: The Froude number divides them — above 1.0 is supercritical, below is subcritical.

twist.text: A hydraulic jump is the violent transition from supercritical to subcritical flow.

climax.text: Stilling basins at dam bases force hydraulic jumps to dissipate energy safely.

punchline.text: The jump is chaos, but it converts destructive energy into harmless turbulence.

quiz.question: What is a hydraulic jump?
options: Water leaping over an obstacle in the channel
The abrupt transition from fast, shallow flow to slow, deep flow
A sudden increase in water speed at a channel constriction

details.summary: Critical flow occurs when the Froude number equals one, representing the transition between tranquil subcritical flow and rapid supercritical flow. Hydraulic jumps form when supercritical flow is forced to decelerate to subcritical conditions.
details.whyItMatters: Understanding critical flow and hydraulic jumps is essential for designing spillways, stilling basins, and channel transitions. Uncontrolled energy dissipation from hydraulic jumps can destroy downstream infrastructure.
takeaways: Critical flow occurs at minimum specific energy for a given discharge
Hydraulic jumps dissipate kinetic energy through turbulence as flow transitions from supercritical to subcritical
Stilling basins are designed to contain hydraulic jumps and protect downstream channels

faq.question: What is the Froude number and why does it matter?
faq.answer: The Froude number is the ratio of flow velocity to wave propagation speed. When less than one, flow is subcritical and waves can travel upstream. When greater than one, flow is supercritical and disturbances cannot propagate upstream.

faq.question: Why are hydraulic jumps both useful and dangerous?
faq.answer: Jumps dissipate energy that would otherwise erode downstream channels and structures. Engineers deliberately create jumps in stilling basins below dam spillways.
